Module 0

The lab

This module sets up everything the other modules use: the two source trees at fixed commits, MS-DOS 4.00 built from its own source code and booted from a disk image, and a FreeBSD 15.1 machine. Everything about MS-DOS in this module was run on the course author's machine; commands and outputs shown are real.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.06 source listings1 exercisesabout 30 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • Get the MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1 sources at the exact commits the course cites, and follow a citation from the notes to the source line.
  • Build MS-DOS 4.00 from source with its original 1988 toolchain, and explain the four problems the build scripts have to work around in the 2024 source release.
  • Make a bootable floppy image and explain why its layout is constrained by the boot sector.
  • Run MS-DOS 4.00 interactively and unattended, and capture program output.
  • Install a FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine that boots through the BIOS, with its source tree in /usr/src.
  • Move a disk image between the two systems and inspect it with tools on both sides.

Prerequisites.

  • A Windows, Linux or macOS computer with Python 3.10 or later and git.
  • About 5 GB of free disk space, most of it for the FreeBSD virtual machine.

0.2 The sources and how the notes cite them#

Every statement in this course about what the code does is tied to a specific line in a specific version. The two trees are pinned:

Project Repository Pinned at
MS-DOS 4.00 github.com/microsoft/MS-DOS, folder v4.0 commit 2d04cacc5322951f187bb17e017c12920ac8ebe2
FreeBSD 15.1 github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src tag release/15.1.0, commit 96841ea08dcfa84b954a32dc5ae1a26c28966cf4

The FreeBSD release itself records the same commit: the REVISION file next to the 15.1 release files on download.freebsd.org contains 96841ea08dcf, and GITBRANCH contains releng/15.1.

Fetch both trees into src-ext/ from the root of the course repository. On Windows:

Terminal
PS> .\tools\fetch_sources.ps1
MS-DOS      2d04cacc5322951f187bb17e017c12920ac8ebe2
freebsd-src 96841ea08dcfa84b954a32dc5ae1a26c28966cf4 (release/15.1.0)

On Linux or macOS the script also runs under PowerShell 7 (pwsh). Without PowerShell, the equivalent is:

Shell
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/MS-DOS.git src-ext/MS-DOS
git -C src-ext/MS-DOS checkout 2d04cacc5322951f187bb17e017c12920ac8ebe2
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse --branch release/15.1.0 \
    https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src.git src-ext/freebsd-src
git -C src-ext/freebsd-src sparse-checkout set stand/i386 stand/common stand/libsa stand/lua \
    stand/defaults stand/forth sys/kern sys/sys sys/amd64 sys/x86 sys/i386/include sys/vm \
    sys/fs/msdosfs sys/geom sys/dev/null sys/conf bin/sh sbin/fdisk sbin/init usr.sbin/boot0cfg \
    usr.bin/login usr.bin/alias lib/libc/sys lib/libc/amd64 lib/libsys/amd64 include \
    share/examples/kld share/mk

The FreeBSD tree is a sparse, shallow checkout: only the directories the course reads, without history (tools/fetch_sources.ps1 has the authoritative list). In the FreeBSD virtual machine you will have the complete tree (section 0.6).

Following a citation#

Source listings in the notes look like this:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.1 – The build environment the release expects (SETENV.BAT lines 1-12)Source ↗
@echo off
echo setting up system to build the MS-DOS 4.01 SOURCE BAK...
set CL=
set LINK=
set MASM=
set COUNTRY=usa-ms
set BAKROOT=d:
rem BAKROOT points to the home drive/directory of the sources.
set LIB=%BAKROOT%\src\tools\lib
set INIT=%BAKROOT%\src\tools
set INCLUDE=%BAKROOT%\src\tools\inc
set PATH=%BAKROOT%\src\tools

The link in the caption opens exactly those lines at the pinned commit. A line containing only ⋮ in a listing means that source lines were left out. Every listing in the course is checked mechanically against the pinned sources with tools/check_citations.py, which you can also use to print any range yourself:

Terminal
$ python tools/check_citations.py --excerpt dos v4.0/src/BOOT/MSBOOT.ASM 253 268
$ python tools/check_citations.py --excerpt bsd stand/i386/boot0/boot0.S 1 40

Two conventions of the MS-DOS source are worth knowing before you read it. Change markers such as ;AN000; and ;AC000; at the end of a line mean "new for DOS 4.00" and "changed for DOS 4.00"; the boot sector's revision history spells this out (MSBOOT.ASM lines 51-55). Comments starting with initials, such as J.K., are notes from individual developers. Note also line 2 of Listing 0.1: the build script calls the tree "MS-DOS 4.01", while the release and its boot sector say 4.00. The course uses the name the binaries report, "MS-DOS Version 4.00" (section 0.5).

0.3 Building MS-DOS 4.00 from source#

What is in the tree#

The v4.0/src folder is a complete build tree, including its own compilers:

Folder Contents Module
BOOT The boot sector, MSBOOT.ASM 1
BIOS IO.SYS: loader, resident device drivers, SYSINIT 1, 2
DOS MSDOS.SYS: the kernel (INT 21h services, FAT, buffers, EXEC, memory) 2
CMD The commands: COMMAND.COM, FORMAT, SYS, FDISK, DEBUG, CHKDSK and more 1, 3
DEV Installable device drivers: ANSI.SYS, RAMDRIVE.SYS, SMARTDRV.SYS, DISPLAY.SYS … 2
MEMM EMM386.SYS, a 386 expanded-memory manager running in virtual 8086 mode 2
SELECT The installation program -
INC, H Shared assembler include files and C headers (structures used by everything) 1-3
MESSAGES, MAPPER, LIB Message files, helper routines, libraries -
TOOLS The 1988 toolchain: MASM 5.10, CL 5.10, LINK 3.65, NMAKE 1.00.05 and helpers 0

The tools in TOOLS are DOS programs: they need a DOS to run on. The course uses DOSBox-X, an open-source PC emulator with a built-in DOS, to run them. Download DOSBox-X from its official GitHub releases page (github.com/joncampbell123/dosbox-x/releases). The course was tested with the Windows portable build dosbox-x-vsbuild-win64-2026.10.01-portable.zip; on Windows, unzip it into build/tools/dosbox-x/ and the course scripts find it there. On other systems, install DOSBox-X from your package manager and make sure dosbox-x is on the PATH, or set the DOSBOX_X environment variable to its full path.

The original build procedure#

RUNME.BAT in the release describes the build in three steps: set up the environment with SETENV.BAT, run NMAKE at the top level, then collect the binaries with CPY.BAT (RUNME.BAT lines 10-32). The top-level MAKEFILE enters each part in turn and runs NMAKE there (MAKEFILE lines 5-24), and CPY.BAT lists the 62 files that make up the product (CPY.BAT).

Four problems, and how the course scripts solve them#

Followed literally, that procedure does not work on the source as published in 2024. The script tools/prepare_dos_build.py makes a build copy of the tree in build/dos4/SRC and fixes four problems. None of the fixes changes what the code does.

Problem Symptom Fix
Line endings: git stores the files with LF line endings; the 1988 tools expect CR LF Assembler and NMAKE errors Convert every text file to CR LF. Files are classed as text or binary by content, not extension (see below)
20 files contain U+FFFD, the Unicode replacement character, where the original had code page 437 box-drawing characters getmsg.asm(473): error A2106: Line too long Map each U+FFFD back to a single byte (?). The original characters are lost; only comments, %OUT build messages and the installer's screens are affected
SETENV.BAT points LIB and INCLUDE at tools\lib and tools\inc (Listing 0.1), which do not exist; the C headers and libraries are in TOOLS\BLD\INC and TOOLS\BLD\LIB C compiler cannot find stdio.h and libraries Generate BUILD.BAT with the corrected paths
File times: DOSBox-X stamps the files it creates with its own clock, which can be behind the host's clock NMAKE thinks fresh outputs are older than the sources and rebuilds them; the second run of the message tool NOSRVBLD hangs Give all copied sources a fixed past date (25 April 2024)

The damaged line that stops the first build is GETMSG.ASM line 473: a comment that was a row of box-drawing characters and is now 66 replacement characters of three bytes each.

The content-based text test matters for two small files that are not source code. Some makefiles feed a file to EXE2BIN's standard input to answer its prompt for a base segment:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.2 – A makefile answers a prompt from a file (MAKEFILE lines 38-41)Source ↗
display.sys: display.obj init.obj parser.obj display.lnk makefile zero.dat
        link @display.lnk
        exe2bin display.exe display.sys < zero.dat
        del display.exe

In the repository ZERO.DAT holds the character 0 followed by a bare line feed. EXE2BIN reads its answer with DOS line input, which ends at a carriage return, so with a bare line feed it waits forever. Converted to 0 CR LF, it works. BIOS\LOCSCR plays the same role for IO.SYS.

The file-time problem shows how NMAKE decides what to rebuild: only by comparing modification times. The rules for message files live in TOOLS.INI:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.3 – Inference rules for message files (TOOLS.INI lines 60-67)Source ↗
.exe.com:
        reloc $*.exe $*.com

.skl.cl1:
        nosrvbld $*.skl $(msg)\$(COUNTRY).msg

.skl.ctl:
        buildmsg $(msg)\$(COUNTRY) $*.skl

A .skl "skeleton" file lists the messages a program uses; NOSRVBLD and BUILDMSG turn it, together with the country's message file USA-MS.MSG, into include files (.CL1, .CTL and others) that the assembler reads. When the generated files look older than COMMAND.SKL, NMAKE runs the rule again. We did not investigate why NOSRVBLD then stops responding; with consistent times it is never run twice.

Running the build#

Terminal
$ python tools/build_dos.py
build/dos4: 1225 text files converted to CRLF (20 repaired from UTF-8), 55 binary files copied
build finished in 1.7 min; 0 error lines; 62/62 CPY.BAT outputs present

build_dos.py runs prepare_dos_build.py, starts DOSBox-X with build/dos4 mounted as drive D:, runs the generated BUILD.BAT (one NMAKE per directory, in the order of the original makefiles), waits for it to finish, and checks the log build/dos4/BUILD.LOG and the 62 outputs listed in CPY.BAT. The time above is from the author's laptop. Two kinds of message in the log are expected. ***** Possible stack size error in ... is printed by the sources themselves: the EndProc macro warns at assembly time when a procedure's pushes and pops do not appear to balance (DOSMAC.INC lines 150-159). LINK : warning L4021: no stack segment appears for programs that are converted to .COM files or device drivers, which do not have a stack segment of their own.

The three files that make up the operating system proper, as built:

File Size (bytes) Built in What it is
IO.SYS 33,321 BIOS Loader, resident drivers and SYSINIT (Module 1)
MSDOS.SYS 37,376 DOS The kernel (Module 2)
COMMAND.COM 37,556 CMD\COMMAND The shell (Module 3)

The boot sector is built too, but not as a file of its own on the disk:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.4 – The boot sector becomes an include file (MAKEFILE lines 20-25)Source ↗
msboot.bin: msboot.obj
        link msboot;
        exe2bin msboot.exe msboot.bin
        dbof msboot.bin boot.inc 7c00 200
        copy boot.inc $(inc)
        del boot.inc

MSBOOT.ASM is assembled at origin 0x7C00, the address where the BIOS will load it. DBOF cuts the 0x200 (512) bytes starting at offset 0x7C00 out of the binary and writes them as assembler data into BOOT.INC. FORMAT and SYS both include that file (MSFOR.ASM lines 199-200, SYS1.ASM lines 261-263): the boot sector travels inside the programs that write it to disks. The same trick puts the master boot record inside FDISK (Module 1).

0.4 A bootable floppy image#

To boot our DOS we need a disk with the boot sector in sector 0 and the system files on it. On a real PC that is the job of FORMAT /S or SYS, which are DOS programs; we would need a running DOS to run them. The script tools/make_floppy.py plays their role instead and writes a 1.44 MB floppy image directly.

The layout cannot be arbitrary, because the boot sector is only 512 bytes and makes strong assumptions:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.5 – The boot sector checks the first two directory entries (MSBOOT.ASM lines 253-268)Source ↗
; Now we scan for the presence of IBMBIO  COM and IBMDOS  COM.  Check the
; first directory entry.
;
        MOV     DI,BX
        MOV     CX,11
        MOV     SI,OFFSET BIO           ; point to "ibmbio  com"
        REPZ    CMPSB                   ; see if the same
        JNZ     CKERR                   ; if not there advise the user
;
; Found the BIOS.  Check the second directory entry.
;
        LEA     DI,[BX+20h]
        MOV     SI,OFFSET DOS           ; point to "ibmdos  com"
        MOV     CX,11
        REPZ    CMPSB
        JZ      DoLoad

The comments say IBMBIO COM, the names in IBM's version. Which names are compared depends on a build switch:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 0.6 – Two products from one source (MSBOOT.ASM lines 500-506)Source ↗
        IF IBMCOPYRIGHT
BIO     DB      "IBMBIO  COM"
DOS     DB      "IBMDOS  COM"
        ELSE
BIO     DB      "IO      SYS"
DOS     DB      "MSDOS   SYS"
        ENDIF

Our build is Microsoft's: the assembled boot sector contains IO SYS and MSDOS SYS, and its OEM name field reads MSDOS4.0. Names are stored as 8 + 3 characters padded with spaces, exactly as in a directory entry, so REPZ CMPSB can compare 11 bytes directly.

So the image builder must:

  1. Put IO.SYS in the first root directory entry and MSDOS.SYS in the second (Listing 0.5). The volume label therefore comes third.
  2. Start IO.SYS at the first data sector, contiguously for at least its first three sectors. The boot sector reads IBMLOADSIZE = 3 sectors from the start of the data area without consulting the FAT (MSBOOT.ASM line 68, lines 296-324). Those three sectors contain a small loader that reads the rest of IO.SYS (Module 1).
  3. Fill in the BIOS Parameter Block (BPB) of the boot sector for a 1.44 MB disk. The BPB fields start at offset 0x0B of the sector (MSBOOT.ASM lines 106-129); the values in the source are placeholders that FORMAT overwrites.
BPB field (MSBOOT.ASM name) Value in the source Value for a 1.44 MB disk
Bytes per sector (ByteSec) 512 512
Sectors per cluster 8 1
Reserved sectors (cSecRes) 1 1
Number of FATs (cFat) 2 2
Root directory entries (DirNum) 512 224
Total sectors (cTotSec) 4*17*305-1 = 20739 2880
Media byte (MEDIA) 0F8h (hard disk) 0F0h
Sectors per FAT (cSecFat) 8 9
Sectors per track (SECLIM) 17 18
Heads (HDLIM) 4 2
Boot drive (Phydrv) 80h (first hard disk) 00h (first floppy)

With these values the disk has 1 boot sector, two FATs of 9 sectors, and a root directory of 14 sectors (224 entries of 32 bytes), so the data area, and IO.SYS, starts at sector 33.

Terminal
$ python tools/make_floppy.py
build/images/dos400.img: 64 files, 1,180,672 bytes used, 276,992 bytes free

The image contains the three system files, a short CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT, and all the programs and drivers from CPY.BAT, including DEBUG.COM, EDLIN.COM, FDISK.EXE, FORMAT.COM, SYS.COM, CHKDSK.COM, MEM.EXE and SORT.EXE.

0.5 Running MS-DOS 4.00#

Interactively#

Terminal
$ python tools/dos_run.py
created build/images/dos400.img
booting build/images/dos400.img (changes are saved to the image; close the window to stop)

DOSBox-X starts with its own built-in DOS, mounts the image as drive A: and runs BOOT A:, which loads sector 0 of the image to 0000:7C00 and jumps to it, exactly as a PC BIOS does. From that moment the built-in DOS is gone: the machine runs our boot sector, our IO.SYS, our MSDOS.SYS and our COMMAND.COM. Changes you make (new files, an edited CONFIG.SYS) are written to the image. Use --image to keep several images, and delete an image to start again from a clean one.

Unattended, with captured output#

For experiments and homework it is easier to run commands and get their output as text:

Terminal
$ python tools/dos_run.py "VER" "CHKDSK A:" "DIR *. | SORT"
Output 0.1 – MS-DOS 4.00, built from source, running three commands
---- VER

MS-DOS Version 4.00
---- CHKDSK A:

Volume DOS400LAB   created 04-25-2024 12:00p
Volume Serial Number is 1988-0400

   1457664 bytes total disk space
     71168 bytes in 3 hidden files
   1109504 bytes in 62 user files
    276992 bytes available on disk

       512 bytes in each allocation unit
      2847 total allocation units on disk
       541 available allocation units on disk

    655360 total bytes memory
    581552 bytes free
---- DIR *.  (pipe)  SORT


        2 File(s)     276480 bytes free
 Directory of  A:\
 Volume in drive A is DOS400LAB
 Volume Serial Number is 1988-0400
17142B4A             0 11-08-26  11:20p
17142B55             0 11-08-26  11:20p

dos_run.py writes a temporary AUTOEXEC.BAT that runs each command with its output redirected to the serial port COM1, and tells DOSBox-X to write everything sent to COM1 into a file. Look at the last command: DIR *. lists files without an extension, and two such files exist while it runs, with zero bytes and names made of hexadecimal digits. Nothing created them except the pipe itself. Module 3 explains them.

Options: --file A:\NAME.EXT=path copies a file from your computer into the root directory first (for example a program you assembled, or your own CONFIG.SYS; with nothing after = it removes the file), --keep image.img saves the disk afterwards so you can inspect what the commands wrote, --show shows the emulator window, --timeout stops a run that waits for input, and --conf-extra SECTION.KEY=VALUE changes the emulated PC for one run (for example --conf-extra cpu.cputype=286 or --conf-extra dosbox.memsize=1; Module 8 uses it). Messages printed before AUTOEXEC.BAT runs (by SYSINIT, for example) are not captured; tools/screen.asm is a short program that copies the text screen to the output, so running it as the first command captures them too.

Because the commands run from AUTOEXEC.BAT, a batch file of your own must be started with CALL NAME or COMMAND /C NAME: a batch file that starts another one without CALL hands over control for good, so the commands after it never run and dos_run.py waits until --timeout. Output also travels at the serial port's speed, about 240 bytes per second (a 4,800-byte TYPE takes 20 seconds), so for long output redirect it to a file, add --keep, and read the file from the saved image.

Your own programs#

nasm assembles .COM programs for DOS directly:

Example 0.1 – A complete DOS program in NASM syntax (hello.asm)
        org     0x100           ; .COM programs are loaded at offset 100h, after the PSP
        mov     dx, msg
        mov     ah, 0x09        ; INT 21h function 09h: write a '$'-terminated string
        int     0x21
        mov     ax, 0x4C00      ; INT 21h function 4Ch: terminate with return code 0
        int     0x21
msg     db      "Hello from MS-DOS 4.00", 13, 10, "$"
Terminal
$ nasm -f bin -o hello.com hello.asm
$ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\HELLO.COM=hello.com "HELLO"
---- HELLO
Hello from MS-DOS 4.00

nasm is available from nasm.us, from most Linux and macOS package managers, and as a FreeBSD package.

The 1988 toolchain: dos_tools.py#

The MS-DOS source tree contains the compilers it was built with, so you can also write DOS programs in C or in MASM syntax with the tools of the time: Microsoft C 5.10 (CL), the Macro Assembler 5.10 (MASM), LINK, LIB and EXE2BIN. tools/dos_tools.py runs them in DOSBox-X on a folder of your computer, which it mounts as drive D:; the toolchain is drive T:, with INCLUDE and LIB set to the corrected paths of section 0.3. DOS text files need CR LF line endings.

Example 0.2 – A complete DOS program in C (HELLO.C, saved with CR LF line endings in build/tmp-00)
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("Hello from Microsoft C 5.10\n");
    return 0;
}

CL compiles and links it in one step; then the program runs on MS-DOS 4.00:

Terminal
$ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir build/tmp-00 "CL HELLO.C"
---- CL HELLO.C
HELLO.C

Microsoft (R) Overlay Linker  Version 3.65
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1983-1988.  All rights reserved.

Object Modules [.OBJ]: HELLO.OBJ
Run File [HELLO.EXE]: HELLO.EXE /NOI
List File [NUL.MAP]: NUL
Libraries [.LIB]:
$ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\HELLO.EXE=build/tmp-00/HELLO.EXE "HELLO"
---- HELLO
Hello from Microsoft C 5.10

The tools run on DOSBox-X's built-in DOS, not on our MS-DOS 4.00: about 1.5 MB of compilers do not fit on the lab floppy next to the system. The programs they produce are ordinary DOS programs, and you always run them on MS-DOS 4.00 with dos_run.py --file. Modules 4, 5 and 9 use this toolchain; Module 5 explains what CL and LINK do in each step.

Debugging#

DOSBox-X has a built-in debugger: its command-line help lists -break-start ("Break into debugger at startup"). The boot-sector tracing exercise in Module 1 (Exercise 1.2) uses a second emulator, QEMU, with GDB, and DOSBox-X's debugger as the alternative: qemu-system-i386 -fda build/images/dos400.img boots the same image, and with the extra options -s -S QEMU waits for a GDB connection on TCP port 1234 before it runs the first instruction.

0.6 The FreeBSD 15.1 machine#

The course's FreeBSD machine is a virtual machine running the official FreeBSD 15.1 disk image. Everything in this section was done on the course author's Windows 11 PC with Hyper-V, and every FreeBSD output in the course was captured in that machine. Other hypervisors work too (see the end of this section), but only the Hyper-V procedure was tested.

Which kind of virtual machine#

Module 1 studies how a PC boots through the BIOS, so the FreeBSD machine must boot that way too:

  • Hyper-V: a Generation 1 virtual machine. Generation 2 machines boot through UEFI.
  • QEMU: the default firmware (SeaBIOS) is a BIOS.
  • VirtualBox, VMware: leave EFI disabled in the machine settings.

Give it 2 CPUs, 2 GB of memory and a 20 GB disk.

Creating the machine (Hyper-V)#

  1. With your browser, download FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.vhd.xz (665 MB) and CHECKSUM.SHA256 from https://download.freebsd.org/releases/VM-IMAGES/15.1-RELEASE/amd64/Latest/.

  2. In Windows PowerShell, as a member of the "Hyper-V Administrators" group, run the course script with the image's hash from CHECKSUM.SHA256:

    Terminal
    PS> .\tools\new_bsd_vm.ps1 -ImageXz $HOME\Downloads\FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-ufs.vhd.xz -Sha256 a6b6632af7d6308008850480c1c9f1b0730455baa6351de517f226a2aa7c840b

    The script checks the hash, decompresses the image (2.5 GB), converts it to VHDX, enlarges it to 20 GB, creates the Generation 1 machine FreeBSD151-Course on Hyper-V's "Default Switch" (which gives it an address by DHCP and Internet access through the host), takes a checkpoint and starts it.

  3. Open the console (vmconnect.exe localhost FreeBSD151-Course). The first boot enlarges the root file system to fill the 20 GB disk and ends at a login: prompt. Log in as root; the official images have no root password at the console.

Check what you are running, and how the disk is laid out:

Output 0.2 – The course VM after its first boot (FreeBSD 15.1)
# freebsd-version -kru; uname -a
15.1-RELEASE
15.1-RELEASE
15.1-RELEASE
FreeBSD freebsd 15.1-RELEASE FreeBSD 15.1-RELEASE releng/15.1-n283562-96841ea08dcf GENERIC amd64
# gpart show
=>      34  41942966  da0  GPT  (20G)
        34       121    1  freebsd-boot  (61K)
       155     66584    2  efi  (33M)
     66739   2097152    3  freebsd-swap  (1.0G)
   2163891  39775053    4  freebsd-ufs  (19G)
  41938944      4056       - free -  (2.0M)

The uname line names the exact source commit the release was built from, 96841ea08dcf: the commit the course cites. The disk is partitioned with GPT and has both a 61 KB freebsd-boot partition (for BIOS boot, holding gptboot, Module 1) and an EFI partition (for UEFI boot); sysctl machdep.bootmethod prints BIOS on a Generation 1 machine.

Tools and sources#

Still as root on the console, install the course's packages and fetch the source tree at the release tag:

Shell
pkg install git-lite nasm gdb
git clone --depth 1 --branch release/15.1.0 https://git.FreeBSD.org/src.git /usr/src
git -C /usr/src rev-parse HEAD   # must print 96841ea08dcfa84b954a32dc5ae1a26c28966cf4

(pkg installs its own package manager the first time; answer y. git clone takes a few minutes and prints a harmless warning that the tag "is not a commit": release/15.1.0 is an annotated tag.) truss, ktrace/kdump, procstat, dtrace, gpart, mdconfig, boot0cfg, readelf, objdump and hexdump are part of the base system. Their manual pages (man truss, man 8 boot0cfg, and man 9 ... for kernel interfaces) are part of the course reading.

If freebsd-version reports a patch level such as 15.1-RELEASE-p3, security updates have been applied to the binaries. The sources the course cites are those of release/15.1.0; for the code studied in this course that difference does not matter, but keep it in mind if you compare a binary with the source byte for byte.

Working from the host: SSH and bsd_run.py#

Typing everything on the VM console is tiring. The course tools use SSH with a key that only this machine accepts. On the host, create the key (press Enter twice for an empty passphrase):

Terminal
PS> ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f build\freebsd\vm\id_course -C dos-bsd-course

Then, on the VM console, install the public key (type it from build\freebsd\vm\id_course.pub), allow root to log in with keys only, and start sshd:

Shell
mkdir -p /root/.ssh && chmod 700 /root/.ssh
echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... dos-bsd-course' > /root/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys
printf 'PermitRootLogin prohibit-password\nPasswordAuthentication no\n' >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sysrc sshd_enable=YES && service sshd start

Take a second checkpoint now (Checkpoint-VM -Name FreeBSD151-Course -SnapshotName course-ready): whatever goes wrong later, you can return to this state in seconds. From now on, tools/bsd_run.py runs commands in the VM and prints their output, like dos_run.py does for MS-DOS; it finds the VM's address through Hyper-V and starts the VM if it is off:

Terminal
$ python tools/bsd_run.py "freebsd-version -kru" "ldd /bin/ls"
$ python tools/bsd_run.py --put hello.c:/root/lab/hello.c "cc -o hello hello.c && ./hello"
$ python tools/bsd_run.py --shell

--put and --get copy files with scp; --shell opens an interactive session. The machine is reachable only from your own PC (Hyper-V's Default Switch), and root can log in only with the key.

Other hypervisors#

On QEMU, use the ...-ufs.qcow2.xz image of the same folder; on VirtualBox or VMware, ...-ufs.vmdk.xz; or install from FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-disc1.iso (folder releases/ISO-IMAGES/15.1/, accept the defaults for a UFS installation). These routes were not tested for the course; the steps after the first login are the same. To use bsd_run.py, set BSD_HOST to the machine's address.

Moving the DOS image to FreeBSD#

FreeBSD can read the floppy image directly, through a memory disk backed by the file. Copy the image into the virtual machine and mount it read-only:

Terminal
$ python tools/bsd_run.py --put build/images/dos400.img:/tmp/dos400.img "mdconfig -a -t vnode -f /tmp/dos400.img" "fstyp /dev/md0" "mount -t msdosfs -o ro /dev/md0 /mnt && ls /mnt | wc -l && ls -lo /mnt/IO.SYS /mnt/MSDOS.SYS /mnt/COMMAND.COM" "umount /mnt && mdconfig -d -u 0"
Output 0.3 – The MS-DOS 4.00 floppy image, seen by FreeBSD 15.1
---- mdconfig -a -t vnode -f /tmp/dos400.img
md0
---- fstyp /dev/md0
msdosfs
---- mount -t msdosfs -o ro /dev/md0 /mnt && ls /mnt | wc -l && ls -lo /mnt/IO.SYS /mnt/MSDOS.SYS /mnt/COMMAND.COM
      64
-rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel uarch                37556 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/COMMAND.COM
-r-xr-xr-x  1 root wheel hidden,rdonly,system 33321 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/IO.SYS
-r-xr-xr-x  1 root wheel hidden,rdonly,system 37376 Apr 25  2024 /mnt/MSDOS.SYS
---- umount /mnt && mdconfig -d -u 0

ls -lo shows the DOS attributes as BSD file flags: hidden,rdonly,system on the two system files and the archive bit (uarch) on COMMAND.COM. The MS-DOS kernel and FreeBSD's msdosfs are two independent implementations of the same on-disk format; Module 2 compares them line by line. The same image is also useful raw: hexdump -C -n 512 /tmp/dos400.img shows the boot sector that MS-DOS's MSBOOT.ASM produced.

Keeping the machine safe#

Some homework writes boot code. Do that on memory disks (mdconfig -a -t malloc -s 64m) or on a second virtual disk, never on the disk the virtual machine boots from. Take a checkpoint (Hyper-V) or snapshot (QEMU, VirtualBox) before each lab session.

0.7 Exercise#

Exercise 0.1: Check your lab#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. Fetch the sources and print Listing 0.5 with tools/check_citations.py --excerpt. Open the link in the listing caption and confirm that it shows the same lines.
  2. Build MS-DOS 4.00 with tools/build_dos.py. Record the build time and the SHA-256 hashes of IO.SYS, MSDOS.SYS and COMMAND.COM, and compare them with two classmates. The builds should be identical, byte for byte, on every machine. Explain why: what would have to be different in a build system for two builds of the same source to produce different files? Name two things that commonly make modern builds differ.
  3. Make the floppy image and run VER, MEM and CHKDSK A: unattended.
  4. Assemble Example 0.1, change its message, and run it in MS-DOS 4.00.
  5. Install the FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine, check /usr/src against the pinned commit, and mount the floppy image read-only. Count the files that ls -la /mnt shows and compare with CHKDSK's "3 hidden files" and "62 user files" in Output 0.1. Explain the difference.

Deliverables: a one-page lab report with the outputs of steps 2, 3 and 5, and your program from step 4.

Hints: if a dos_run.py command never finishes, the program is probably waiting for keyboard input; add --show to see the screen. If the build stops, look at the end of build/dos4/BUILD.LOG: the last ===== line tells you which directory was being built.
